text: I started the term barely passing, honestly; the lectures felt uneven week to week, and I’m glad I had a study group because solo I’d have floundered more. Prof. Haddad’s pace and the prerequisite gap didn’t help my weak theory, though the LMS flow kept submissions smooth. I’m still not sure I’d recommend it, but the last stretch fit my tight, full-time-work schedule.

I took Computer Networks with Dr. Singh mainly out of curiosity because I figured it would cover the stuff I’d actually want to understand down the line, and it did fill some gaps you don’t get from the prereq course. The workload felt heavy and time-consuming, especially with the report-heavy assessments that stacked up during midterm crunch week and didn’t ease up after, even though I tried to stay on top of the deadlines. I started off pretty engaged in class, but my attendance faded as the weeks wore on and the tooling quirks made deadlines feel tougher than they needed to be; the platform hiccups often turned simple submissions into a multi-day saga, which didn’t help. Instructions sometimes left a lot to interpretation, and I found myself double-guessing what exactly was expected for the weekly writeups, even though the course technically fills our track’s prerequisites better than I expected. I remember a late fall office-hours session where a TA explained a tricky congestion-control slide twice, which finally clicked for a concrete project detail I had been stuck on, though I wish the cadence hadn’t depended on those ad-hoc moments. Overall, I’d still recommend it to someone pursuing the track, but go in with a sturdier plan for the heavy weeks.

I’m a returning student and felt a little rusty walking into Computer Networks, and that rust showed up in how uneven the week-to-week pace could be. Prof. Cohen is clearly knowledgeable and the lectures land when he’s on, but some weeks the delivery felt scattered and I had to piece things together on my own; I relied on the forums, which are helpful yet can feel a bit dismissive when you ask a basic clarify question. The course as a whole leaned toward individual work, and I used the materials selectively—I mainly revisited the packet flows when I needed to, not as a constant reference. A concrete quirk: the fast-score feedback arrives quickly but the explanations are thin, so I felt a bit left to infer what I could have done better on the midterm. Overall, I’d say it taught me something useful, but I wouldn’t take it again even though it helped me refocus.

Cyber Security Basics, in the middle of a brutal, overbooked semester, felt like a required puzzle I had to fit into my schedule rather than something I was especially excited about. I’ll admit I didn’t click with the way the material is delivered—slides are serviceable but forgettable—and the constant assignment deadlines piled up, which didn’t help when tooling kept acting up and messing with due weeks. I remember an early moment of confusion about what counts as a “threat model,” which shaped how I approached the rest of the term, and I can’t help but think the feedback often arrived too late to adjust the next task. Still, being in this track, it’s hard to ignore that this class did push me toward tighter problem-solving, even if I’d probably skip it next time.

Taking Database Systems as a required course for my track, I felt like Dr. Park kept things steady but didn’t always push us past the basics, which matched my sense of the workload. The forums helped a lot when I was stuck, though sometimes the tone felt a bit dismissive—like if you asked the same question twice you’d get a quick shrug instead of a second read, which didn’t help when the concepts got tangled. Grades mattered more than the volume of work, with only a few assessments, but each one carried real weight, and I ended up aiming for a solid B because that’s where the effort lined up. I appreciated how the prerequisites paid off: the material built on the earlier stuff without feeling like a cliff, and the practical parts—little things like a SQL-ish assignment with a small ER-to-relational draw—felt tangible. I was juggling this with another hard class, so I used the materials selectively, focusing on office hours and the TAs for the stubborn bits, and I still walked away feeling like I had a usable grasp, even if the grading rubric remained vague in spots.

The course was mostly tolerable, but I left with one big nagging thought about how the grading is handled and how little of it feels transparent. I’m in the summer term, the pacing is compressed, and I leaned on recordings and notes far more than live sessions; the way deadlines stacked up felt like a sprint you don’t get warned about, even though I knew it would be project-heavy with high-stakes exams. The instructions often leave too much room for interpretation, which made the prerequisite material feel like a moving target—works best if you already know adjacent material, otherwise you keep spinning. I did appreciate the concrete project I worked on, along with the occasional timely feedback on a code submission, but the quality varies a lot by assignment, and the occasional forum reply from the TA came across as more helpful than official feedback. I remember one office hours chat where I showed a messy confusion about cross-validation and the professor sketched a quick heuristic that finally clicked, which stuck with me longer than most rubric notes. Overall, it’s a solid-but-not-polished advanced elective that demands you stay on top of the structure rather than trust the prompts alone.

Took Linear Algebra as an advanced elective last semester, and the grade felt like it matched the effort I put in, though the prerequisite expectations were higher than advertised. The project-heavy format plus rough-to-use software made the slides feel serviceable but not memorable; office hours with Dr. Yu helped a ton when I was stuck on a proof.

I signed up for Cyber Security Basics as my main focus this term, since I was coming back after a long stretch and felt rusty, but the summer pace made it feel like I was chasing a moving deadline. The project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams kept me honest, yet the deadlines piled up so fast that I fell behind and only caught up right before the next big submission window. The LMS and submission flow were smooth enough, and I appreciated that scores came quickly, even if the explanations were oddly thin and didn’t help me pinpoint where I went wrong. A turning point around exam week finally clicked one concept for me, but overall I left drained, irritated by the backlog of feedback that came too late to fix anything before the next task. Still, I’d probably tell a friend to try it if they like a crunch.

Machine Learning was a required course for the track, and I started out pretty engaged, but by midsemester my attendance slipped as other demanding classes piled up and I started feeling buried by deadlines. The organization felt off; the weekly plan and due dates didn’t line up neatly, and the admin side kept throwing late feedback that I couldn’t use to adjust in time. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I found myself rereading them alongside the textbook to even grasp what was being asked on the assignments. The forums helped at moments, but some replies felt dismissive, like the TA assumed I should already know the nuance, which dampened my motivation a bit. The toolchain on the platform quirks added unnecessary stress—every time I tried to run a notebook, something failed or reset, and that small friction added up. I remember an early confusion about choosing a reasonable loss function for a simple linear model, which then colored how I approached later topics and made parts of the course feel heavier than they were. Still, I managed to keep pace enough to finish, while balancing it with two tougher courses, and the overall experience left me with a few practical takeaways more than a spark of excitement.

Starting with a complaint: the assessment design felt inconsistent and often rushed, like a few quick quizzes after long gaps. I’m a returning student, rusty, juggling another hard class, and the sparse feedback—mostly nowhere near the deadline—left me frustrated but still pushing through.

Calculus II felt like I was juggling with a full-time job and a mid-semester sprint, and the software stack started rough but got usable after a few tortuous evenings. I remember the first week my calculator kept freezing on the integration by parts steps, which colored the rest of the term even as group work finally clicked when our trio finally synced. The quick feedback on problem sets helped, but the explanations were thin, and attendance faded as time got tight. I wouldn’t recommend it, though there were moments

Data Structures with Prof. Haddad ended up being the main thing I did this term, since it’s required for the track and I squeezed it in with another tough class. The lectures explained the concepts well enough, but I kept wishing the real-world examples weren’t so thin; I left more with “the idea” than something I could actually apply. The workload was heavy and almost all the deadlines piled up—assignments every week, with a big one due right after midterms that felt rushed. I tried to keep up, but when deadlines hit the email support from the TA felt slow, I’d send a question and end up waiting, which stressed me out more than the material did. My group interactions with peers were the bright spot; we actually helped each other parse confusing parts and I came away feeling less alone grinding through pointers and arrays. The grading rubric, though, felt vague, which didn’t help when I was unsure how to gauge if a submission was on the right track. I’m not sure I’d recommend it without better pacing and clearer guidance, especially since I tackled it alongside another hard class and was basically running on fumes by the end.

Dr. Chen’s Linear Algebra was fine for work-readiness vibes, but I won’t take it again. The lectures are dry, and the course dumps a heavy report focus as deadlines creep in, with unclear collaboration norms and a sharp ramp after an accessible start.

I’m new to the discipline, and the summer term with the compressed pacing made Machine Learning feel doable at first and then suddenly overwhelming, especially as the assignments piled up with tight deadlines. Prof. Alvarez delivers clear lectures, and the pacing is decent at times, but the course design leaned heavy on frequent submissions, which stressed me out as I fell behind and then tried to catch up right before deadlines. Office hours felt like a rescue—one session I went in with a foggy data pipeline issue and walked out with a concrete plan, which saved the week. I remember an early confusion about overfitting that tangled into the rest of the term, shaping how I approached each new topic, even as the early material seemed accessible enough.

Taking Computer Networks as an advanced elective felt like stepping into a fast-moving lab where I mostly kept up by patching gaps in my basics rather than mastering theory up front. My strong coding background helped me parse the stack stuff, but the theory bits still tripped me up, and the early weeks with the rough-on-setup tools made the first few labs feel heavier than they should have been. The quick feedback helped though; when I hit a bug in the packet tracing script, Prof. Haddad’s comments arrived fast enough to pivot, which kept the momentum from stalling. The platform started off feeling clunky—configurations and the VM images were finicky—but by week four it settled into something workable, and I could focus more on the design choices than the install ritual. I compared it to another term’s course and realized this one leans more into building from the prerequisites, which is fine, just not as forgiving when deadlines stack up and you’re juggling four problems at once. Office hours felt like a rescue squad, a place to vent about the timing and get a concrete nudge on where to tighten the next submission, which kept me from dropping the thread entirely. One project stood out in memory—a graph-traffic simulator that demanded a clever tweak to the timing model—an incidental moment that stuck, even as I wished the course had a little more breathing room.

Calculus II felt like a required maze this semester: the pacing was fine most weeks, but when I had two hard classes at once, I could feel the momentum slipping and attendance fade a bit. The software stack started rough, then settled, and the feedback varied a lot by assignment, which made it hard to trust early quizzes. Our group collaboration was supposed to help, but the expectations felt unclear, and communications sometimes dragged, yet I still pulled through with enough time and a stubborn streak.

In Dr. Miller’s Database Systems course, I felt rusty but went in hoping it’d help with industry work; the slides are serviceable, feedback arrives quickly enough to adjust, and I barely passed after struggling most of the term, especially since office hours once helped me untangle a project deadline.

I took Machine Learning while juggling a full-time job, and the lecturer kept things clear even as I sailed through new basics. The materials, though, felt spotty and I only used them when deadlines loomed; the weekly assignments piled up fast and the feedback varied a lot, which made pacing tricky. I’d say it’s a solid B with enough support if you already have a plan and don’t mind chasing answers by email when a deadline sneaks up.

I took Database Systems in my last semester before graduating, mainly because I needed it for a specialization, and I’m glad I did, even though I’m not sure I’d take it again. Prof. Haddad’s lectures were solid enough, and the slides helped when I pulled them up, but they’re not exactly memorable—more a dependable map than a destination. The tooling setup was a pain at first, which made the early weeks frustrating, even though the actual tools work fine once you get through the hiccups. I found the course material useful for filling some gaps I had, and the peer help between us classmates was basically how I kept afloat. One week, the exam week felt oddly memorable—an unexpectedly straightforward short answer section that made me rethink how I’d been studying, which stuck with me as a weirdly positive takeaway. Overall, it’s not a slam dunk, but it did what I needed.

Prof. Alvarez’s lectures are clear and the pacing decent, but the deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and I relied mostly on recordings and notes. The LMS flows smoothly, office hours actually rescued me, and group study helps, though I wouldn’t fully recommend the course.

Calculus II with Dr. Singh was made real for me mostly by the peer discussions, which I found helped more than the official materials, since I’m comfortable with proofs but not so much with the systems work the lectures drift toward. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and I did notice that the quick feedback comes fast, but the explanations behind the marks aren’t there to my taste, which left me juggling gaps I didn’t expect. The tool setup for the platform felt like a sink-or-swim hurdle, and the deadlines stacked up in a way that left me tired and a bit resigned by midterm week. Still, the way the instructor talks about how to apply integration techniques in real problems stuck with me, even if the grading felt off.

This Data Structures course hit me where it hurts: I barely scraped by after spending most of the term fighting with proofs and trying to keep up when I’m not a systems person. The lectures and LMS are smooth enough to navigate, and I did use the materials when I needed them, but the few assessments mattered so much that I felt like I couldn’t afford to miss a beat. I leaned on a lot of peer help more than staff office hours, and I still remember one chaotic forum thread where my classmate explained a tricky recurrence relation in plain terms that finally clicked after three sleepless nights. Compared to the same term’s other course, this one demanded more stubborn persistence, and even though it did fill some gaps in prerequisites, I don’t think I’d sign up for it again.

I started the Linear Algebra term feeling confident with proofs, but midway through I faded on attendance and relied on my peers more than the staff. The early confusion about basis vectors stuck with me and colored the rest of the term, even as the slides stayed serviceable.

I took Operating Systems mainly to fit my schedule, since I already have a solid coding background but weaker grasp of the theory, and Dr. Singh’s class felt more like a slog than a structured learning path. The lectures were strong on big-picture concepts, but the real gaps showed up in the hands-on parts—the examples didn’t land for me, and tooling problems dragged deadlines into weeks where I already felt stretched. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, with office hours occasionally saving the week; I remember one forum post where Dr. Singh walked through a tricky mutex issue, but that rescue felt loud against the overall confusion. The grading rubric felt vague, and the midterm format was odd enough to throw me off, so I wouldn’t push this on someone looking for asmooth, coherent growth arc.

Calculus II bumped from interesting to a slog pretty quickly for me. I started out engaged, but the attendance faded as the built-in tool setup and dense problem sets ate into study time; the platform and tooling felt like more hassle than help, even though the content was solid. I did like the early prerequisites, and I kept grinding toward the late-semester turning point where I finally saw how the ideas connected, but the quick feedback with thin explanations left me craving more guidance from TAs during office hours.

Took Database Systems in my first semester while juggling a full-time job, so the workload felt heavy but manageable once I found a rhythm; the quick feedback helped me adjust even as I struggled with the tooling setup that kept stalling my first few submissions. The LMS flow was smooth, but the deadlines stacked up more than I expected, and most of the work stayed solo with little peer interaction—made an early project feel like a solo sprint. One memorable week was that exam on week eight, when the questions clicked after I finally carved out a solid block of time.

Honestly, as someone new to the discipline, the Database Systems course laid out the basics clearly enough, and I appreciated the big-picture explanations even when the concrete examples felt thin. The tooling setup and deadline weeks were rough, though, and that friction tinted my week-to-week regardless of the solid prereqs. Still, the lectures clicked at the right pace, and I’d generally recommend it to others juggling a heavy load.

I enrolled in Operating Systems mainly to satisfy a specialization requirement, and Dr. Singh is clearly competent and genuinely enthusiastic, which kept me oddly hopeful even as the course stretched my limits. The early weeks were engaging, but the ramp-up hit hard and attendance waned as the semester wore on, especially with the assignment-heavy pace and a cluster of deadlines that stacked up unexpectedly. I started out keeping up, then felt pulled between this and two other demanding courses, and the tooling setup for submission and environment configuration was frustrating enough to sour the momentum. Feedback quality varies a lot by assignment, and some weeks I’d get quick notes while others felt like they were edited in a rush, which didn’t help planning my study time. Still, Dr. Singh’s lectures remained clear when the topics clicked, and I left with a better grasp of process scheduling and memory management than I expected.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester, and I’m still rusty, so I rely mostly on recordings and notes from Prof. Haddad’s Machine Learning class. The setup to get the tooling running felt like a detour that didn’t pay off every week, and I’m not always sure the feedback timing matched the assignment load. A study group helped, but I still felt the pacing and prerequisites built up in a way that made the middle stretch feel rough but doable. The project and deadlines were real,

The Database Systems course fit my full-time work, with a heavy, deadline-driven pace and a few late nights catching up around deadlines; the instructor spoke clearly, but the grading felt finicky, and platform quirks added avoidable stress during the summer term.

Summer term in Computer Networks with Dr. Chen dragged on despite quick feedback, and the recordings were useful but mostly dry. It was my main focus, and the material clicked only after I already knew some adjacent topics, so the organization felt messy and the support, though quick, was still frustrating.

Last semester in Linear Algebra with Prof. Rios felt like a near-miss: it checked the boxes I needed for my schedule but left me with a few nagging gaps. The concepts came through clearly in theory, but the examples in class were thin and didn’t always translate to the problem sets I struggled with while juggling another hard course. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped, yet the grading rubric felt vague and left me guessing how parts of my work would be evaluated. When deadlines hit, email support was slow to respond, which was frustrating, especially as I tried to plan around back-to-back finals. Still, I managed to push through the last few weeks, balancing it with the other demanding classes, and there were moments that stuck with me afterward.

The Operating Systems course was okay for what I needed to fit my schedule, but I felt I worked through it more out of habit than interest. The conceptual explanations clicked more than the concrete examples, and the feedback on assignments varied a lot, which didn’t help during the rough mid-semester crunch. I’d say it’s best if you already know related material and can tolerate some ambiguity about collaboration and deadlines.

I took Linear Algebra while juggling a full-time job and tried to fit study into those short evening sessions, which made the workload feel relentless and the early weeks especially brutal. My memory keeps returning to that first confused moment in week two when we went from vector spaces to eigen stuff in a single lecture and I stared at the screen like a deer, which oddly colored how I approached almost every later assignment. The course was very assignment-heavy, with deadlines piling up and the stack of problem sets feeling like a slow drip, and I would be racing to get them done after dinner while still staying awake; the software stack we used started rough—lots of import errors and unclear expectations—but once I pinned down a workflow it became a bit more manageable. I found the prerequisite gaps pointed out by the instructor surprisingly helpful, but the grading rubric never quite clicked for me, which left me guessing on what counted in the final grade and nudged my motivation down despite genuine curiosity about the theory. By midterm I could tell attendance faded as the pace got heavier, and that lingering early confusion shaped how I interpreted later topics, even when the concepts finally started to click. Overall, there are real value moments, but I can’t confidently recommend it to someone who needs a smooth, transparent path to a good grade.

Machine Learning felt like chasing a moving target this term. With a full-time job, I mostly stuck to recordings and notes, and the weeks where lecture delivery seemed uneven didn’t help; feedback often arrived too late to adjust, especially during the midterm scramble. I remember the week of the big data project where the rubric shifted last minute, which didn’t help my already tight schedule. The vibe was that help from staff was sparse compared to how much students were tutoring each other.

I’m new to OS and made it my main focus this term, and the lectures helped only so far; the tools glitch stressed me out, but peer chats were surprisingly helpful, especially since I’m still figuring basics, and the grade felt like a guess more than real understanding.

Calculus II was a slog that I kept up with almost every lecture, but I never felt the vibe click the way it should in an intro service course. Prof. Alvarez is clearly capable, yet the delivery left me dry and a bit exhausted—the recorded lectures are useful, sure, but they feel more like a lecture-on-rails than a discussion, which makes motivation jittery when you’re juggling another hard class. The platform quirks were another constant stressor: a recurring glitch during a live Q&A that ate into a lot of study time, and the weird auto-updates right when I was trying to pull together notes. TAs were practical and responsive, which helped when the homework clock kept ticking and I needed a quick sanity check on a rotation of trigonometric integrals, but the feedback timing varied a lot by assignment, so I spent more guessing than learning between due dates. I remember one week around week five, when the project-style week with multiple mini-deadlines felt doable but then the grading pattern surprised me with some odd rubric shifts. I had enough time but inconsistent motivation, and by the end I was tired and resigned, wondering how I would tackle the next calculus gauntlet.

Dr. Park’s Calculus II felt organized, with slides that worked as a backbone, but I’m new to the math basics and mostly relied on recordings and notes to keep up; the grading rubric is vague, and office hours rescued the whole thing, honestly.

Dr. Chen made Linear Algebra feel doable even with my flaky motivation, and the LMS flows smoothly, but deadlines piled up and feedback arrived late; I barely passed after struggling through the weekly problem sets and the midterm, honestly.

Coming back to Computer Networks with Dr. Park felt like waking up from a long nap and realizing I’d forgotten a lot of the basics, which is why I’m glad I’m in my last semester and chasing a specialization. The early weeks were fine, but the pace kicks up fast and the ramp feels sharper than I expected; I started rusty, and that memory anchor—confusing the difference between ACLs and routing tables at the first lab—stuck with me and colored subsequent weeks. Grading rubrics were vague at first and only clarified after the deadline, which left me guessing if a late submission would still count, even though I did the work. The forums helped sometimes, but the vibe there could be dismissive, and I wish feedback came sooner rather than after the dust settled. Still, I’d recommend it broadly, especially if you’re chasing the specialization, because the core ideas eventually clicked for me.

I’m a returning student who felt a bit rusty, and I kept up with nearly every lecture in Dr. Miller’s Operating Systems, but I kept hitting rough patches as the material jumped from basics to advanced stuff faster than I expected. The tooling and deadline weeks were a slog—submitting in the LMS sometimes felt like a guessing game, and the grading rubric still felt vague to me, even though the comments were detailed after the fact. The course ramps up quickly after a decent start, and I had to juggle full-time work, which made the early weeks the clearest for me and the later weeks more of a grind. One memorable week was the big midterm where I saw a tricky memory management question that stuck with me afterward.

I’m new to the discipline, and the Database Systems course under Dr. Chen felt like a rough start that slowly tightened up. The recorded lectures were useful but dry, and the software stack started rough but became manageable; I remember early confusion around a query optimizer concept that shaped how I approached the rest of the term. The exams seemed fair enough once I saw the pattern, but the quick feedback came with a thin explanation, and the assessment mix didn’t quite map to what we covered in lectures.

I took Computer Networks in my first semester, mostly out of genuine curiosity about how the bits actually travel, and I left feeling tired and a bit resigned more often than not. Prof. Cohen is clear in lectures and the pacing is decent, but the whole assessment setup felt clunky: a few big, make-or-break tasks where missing a single piece of a protocol earns you a big hit, which made the course feel harsher than the peers’ descriptions. The group work can be useful if your team clicks, but on my project we spent more time aligning schedules than debugging a router problem, and I ended up carrying the late-night glue work. The prerequisites fit like a narrower square peg, honestly—you’re best if you already know adjacent material, otherwise the vocabulary alone can swallow you. I did compare this to another course from the term, which moved faster with smaller checks, and that contrast stuck with me as the turning point when I realized I might be in over my head here. By the end, the turning point felt like a rough mid-semester crunch that dragged on, leaving me unsure whether I’d recommend it to someone else.

Linear Algebra with Dr. Miller fit my short evening study slots, and the material was accessible enough, but the ramp-up felt abrupt for my weak theory background; the few major projects mattered a lot, and the tool setup ate into learning time more than I’d like.

I took Cyber Security Basics mainly because it was a prerequisite for the specialization, and I mostly got a solid B that felt like it matched the effort I put in. Dr. Park’s lectures can be uneven week to week, which made it hard to predict what would actually land, but when a topic clicked, it clicked hard and helped me see where I needed to fill gaps in my understanding. The course helped fill prerequisite gaps better than I expected, especially when we tackled the core threat models, and I appreciated that the exam format wasn’t punitive—fair in how it tested the material rather than tricking you with tiny edge cases. I did notice feedback arriving later than I’d hoped, which sometimes meant I’d miss the chance to adjust midstream, a friction that felt avoidable. The study vibe leaned more on peers helping each other than on staff guidance, which kept me moving, but I wished the staff had been a touch more proactive. One memorable week was the midterm where we had a practical section on threat modeling; it stuck with me because I really had to map concepts to a real system on the spot, and that week stands out as a clear mental anchor. Overall, it’s a fair course, just with a few quirks that kept it from feeling perfectly smooth.

I enjoyed the instructor's explanations of concepts, but the material overall felt rough around the edges—the software stack started off clunky and a bit brittle, and I often found my notes sitting on top of shaky recordings rather than clear, usable slides. I mostly relied on recordings and notes because I study in short evening sessions, which makes the assignment-heavy pace with frequent deadlines harder to keep up with; I’m not sure my C grade reflects how well I actually grasped the ideas. Office hours on a Tuesday helped a lot when I could catch them, though the collaboration expectations still felt unclear and the examples didn’t always land for me. Still, I liked the instructor’s vibe enough to stick with it.

Linear Algebra in my first semester was fine for what I needed for the specialization, kept up with nearly every lecture, and the LMS flow was smooth, but I’d still skip it again even though it helped; forums helped, but sometimes felt dismissive when I asked basic questions.

I kept(Database Systems) as my main focus this term, juggling a full-time job and still managing to attend almost every lecture, and I’ll admit the early software stack was rough but became manageable later. The course felt well organized and the materials were solid, though the prerequisite material assumed more prior knowledge than I had, which made the project-heavy workload and high-stakes exams tough. Office hours rescued me more than once, but I’m still torn about whether I’d recommend it.

The Operating Systems course fit into my schedule and gave me a solid A after a curve, with the material surprisingly practical through the TA support and smooth LMS flow. I appreciated that the prerequisites filled in gaps better than I expected, and group work only paid off when the team stayed aligned; deadlines and a couple of tight weeks kept time pressure manageable. Overall, it felt like a balanced but light touch to the tougher topics, with enough real-world flavor to keep it from being abstract.

I started off really into the idea that this Machine Learning course would be useful for real work, but as the semester wore on I found myself losing steam and attendance started to fade, even though I kept coding along at home. Dr. Chen is quick with feedback and you can adjust things fast, which helped a lot early on, but the exams felt like a trap—high-stakes and not clearly aligned with the project work, which left me frustrated and a bit wary about how my efforts would actually pay off. I have a strong coding background but weaker theory, so I leaned on hands-on parts, yet the big project kept throwing curveballs that didn’t always match what the rubric hinted at; the grading rubric itself felt vague enough to make me second-guess what mattered. A late-semester turning point came when I had to defend a model in front of peers and realized I’d learned a ton of practical tricks, even if I didn’t love the overall vibe of the exam fairness. The LMS and submission flow stayed smooth, and the quick turnaround on feedback helped me iterate, but I’m still unsure whether I’d recommend taking it if you’re mainly chasing a tidy, theory-heavy payoff.

Database Systems had clear lectures, but with my full-time job I used the materials only when needed. The platform quirks and slow email support during deadlines added stress, and I felt the prerequisite assumed more background than advertised. One memorable week was the big project, a bit exhausting yet learned a lot.

Prof. Cohen is clearly solid, and I’d say the lectures fit the vibe for an advanced elective: the recorded talks are useful for catching the key ideas, even if they feel a bit dry on refresh. The LMS run smoothly and the submission flow kept me from wasting time; deadlines were predictable, which helped with the usual first-semester time crunch. I thought the collaboration expectations were fuzzy at first, and that plus the way the project pairs were assigned made it hard to gauge who was pulling their weight. Still, the course builds well on the prerequisites, and I ended up understanding the core tools better than I expected—just not sure that understanding fully clicked during the term. Overall, it’s a doable, say-it-plain course with some rough edges and one memorable little coding hiccup I won’t forget.

Summer term was rough in OSes with the compressed pace. I still remember that early confusion about process scheduling that set the tone for the rest of the term, and I barely scraped by despite a lot of late nights. The platform quirks and some sloppy admin notes didn’t help, and while peers helped more than staff, I felt mostly stuck with the workload and mixed feedback across assignments.

Data Structures in my last semester before graduation was a mixed ride. I’m a returning student who feels rusty, and the course starts approachable but ramps up quickly, which left me clinging to forums and office hours more than I’d like. The tool setup felt like a constant bottleneck—getting the IDE, the grader plugin, and the local environment running took more time than the early weeks of learning the data structures themselves, and that ate into actual problem solving. On the plus side, the feedback came fast enough to adjust, and the TAs were responsive and practical about how to fix a failing run or optimize a stubbed function. There’s a real usefulness to the material, even if I didn’t enjoy every moment; it finally clicked that these structures are a toolset, not a parade of theory, especially during the big midterm where the memory-week questions stuck with me. One memorable moment was a debugging sprint during Week 8 that dragged on but taught me to read code paths more carefully.
